title: Leadership learning from experience
author: Nick Hart
summary: Hart continues a series on the hidden, tacit knowledge that separates expert school leaders from merely experienced ones. His central argument is that years in post are a poor proxy for expertise, because two leaders holding the same job for the same length of time in the same school do not have the same experience. Drawing on Bereiter and Scardamalia, he notes that experts keep reinvesting freed-up mental capacity into problems that stretch them while plateaued colleagues recycle problems they have already mastered. He then complicates that tidy distinction in two ways. First, the situations a leader meets are partly a function of context, including cohort stability, safeguarding load and parental temperament, some of which is outside the leader's control and some of which is the delayed consequence of the leader's own earlier decisions. Second, social networks compound the gap, since a role with external networking structures exposes a leader to more viewpoints than one confined to a single building. The piece closes by refusing to leave this to chance and promising a follow-up on deliberate mechanisms to reduce the variation.
points: Hart separates experience from expertise, arguing that a leader who plateaus after two years and one who keeps growing for ten can look identical on paper.
He uses Bereiter and Scardamalia to explain the divide as a choice about what to do with the mental capacity that routine work frees up.
He lists contextual contrasts, from stable cohorts and low turnover to complex safeguarding cases and agitated parent bodies, that give two leaders genuinely different problem sets.
He notes that some apparent bad luck, such as a tense staff room or a change-resistant team, may be a delayed second or third order effect of the leader's own earlier decisions.
He argues that network breadth multiplies exposure, so equally attentive leaders can end up with different amounts of hidden knowledge because one simply had more rooms to be attentive in.
quotes: Expertise and experience are not the same so why is it that one leader developed while the other didn’t? Bereiter and Scardamalia looked at this (albeit not in the domain of school leadership) and found that experts in a domain keep tackling problems that extend them while experienced non experts settle for tackling problems that they have already mastered.

As leaders become more familiar with the tasks they’re responsible for, they typically get more efficient at doing them, at least in terms of the mental capacity required to carry them out. What they do with that freed up capacity is where the divide happens between our two leaders.
We can quantify experience by the number of years doing a job but two leaders doing the same job for the same number of years in the same school will not have an identical experience.

But a tense staff room, an agitated parent body or a team resistant to change could be second or third order consequences of a leader’s own earlier decisions, arriving late enough that the leader no longer recognises their own hand in them.
Yes, expert leaders may choose to tackle problems that extend them but some leaders may never get to experience certain problems because of the context of the school.

Two leaders can be equally attentive, equally willing to seek out an alternative view, and still end up with different amounts of hidden knowledge simply because one of them had more rooms to be attentive in.
If experience and expertise are not the same and some leaders can develop from a similar experience while others don’t, it means that we can’t leave this strand of leadership development to chance.
